page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Find the centres, radii and distance
steps.margin_note: First mark. Both circles are already in standard form, coefficient 1 on x² and y².
steps.why: The centre, radius, and distance-between-centres of both circles are the three ingredients the angle formula needs — each comes directly from reading g, f, c off the two given equations.
common_mistakes: Reading C₁ as (−6, −3) instead of (6, 3) — the centre is (−g, −f), and here g = −6, f = −3, so the centre is (6, 3).
Computing r₂ = √(4 + 9 − 59), forgetting that c = −59 makes the term −c = +59 inside the square root.
steps.memory_tip: d = 10, r₁ = 2, r₂ = √72 — three clean-ish numbers worth double-checking with Pythagoras (6² + 8² = 100) before moving to the angle formula.

steps.label: Apply the angle formula
steps.margin_note: Second mark, for substituting into the angle formula and naming the angle.

lines.text: ∴ Angle between the circles is θ = 45° = π/4

steps.why: Substituting d, r₁, r₂ into cos θ = (d² − r₁² − r₂²) / (2r₁r₂) and simplifying √72 = 6√2 collapses the fraction to the standard value 1/√2, which is cos 45°.
common_mistakes: Leaving √72 unsimplified and failing to spot that 4√72 = 24√2, so the fraction does not reduce.
Computing 100 − 4 − 72 incorrectly as 100 − 76 = 24 miscopied as some other number.
steps.memory_tip: Simplify √72 = √(36 · 2) = 6√2 before doing the division — a surd left unsimplified is the usual reason this fraction looks stuck.
